TRELLIS.2 · mesh ↔ video registration · 2026-08-15

The Rotation Handoff

Guan shipped the exact rotations used to render the Kling input PNGs — re-rendered and verified byte-identical to the shipped images, so ground truth, not estimates. This page is the ground-truth video frame against what those rotations produce, for every object, plus what my own search had found. They recover both objects my search failed on.

Why a search was needed at all, and why it should stop

Our pipeline renders every object through one fixed camera. Guan renders each object from its own upright view, because that is what makes Kling produce a usable video — through our camera the pumpkin is seen from underneath and the horse and penguin are side-on. The orientation gap between those two facts is what the search was trying to close.

It closed it for four of six. It failed on pumpkin_rot, and on teapot_ceramic_crack it produced a pose worse than the one it started from, because a cast shadow in the video pulled it off. Guan's objection — that video models give you shadows, deformation and drift, so orientation should never be inferred from their output — is exactly right.

The convention, and the one correction to his note

His matrices live in a y-up world with the camera on +Z. Ours renders canonical(v), which folds in the axis map M = (−x, z, y). His README suggests conjugating by M R Mᵀ. That is 174° off, because our canonical map and the camera frame change differ by a 180° yaw. The correct form is not a similarity transform:

F = (x, −z, y)   his camera frame -> ours
M = (−x, z, y)   our canonical() axis map

our render      = R_ours · canonical(v)   = R_ours · M · normalize(v)
his pose, ours  = F · R_total · normalize(v)
                                    R_ours = F · R_total · Mᵀ
Confirmed from both directions

Guan's README predicts his rotations sit 5.6–10.8° from the four my search solved. Deriving F·R·Mᵀ independently and measuring gives 5.6, 5.8, 7.0, 10.8° — the same range, to the tenth of a degree. The other candidate forms land at 157–175°.

Gate on coverage, not IoU

His second correction, and it matters more than the first.

blue — both agree
red — our mesh, no video  ← this is the error that matters
green — video, no mesh

A cast shadow only ever adds to the video mask. It can therefore wreck symmetric IoU while leaving our mesh perfectly placed. Coverage asks the one-sided question — what fraction of our silhouette falls outside the video's object — and is immune to it by construction. teapot_ceramic_crack is the proof: IoU 0.682, coverage 2.18%.

Object by object

pumpkin_rot

Guan 0.00% uncovered · IoU 0.9008   mine 10.23% · IoU 0.6923

The one I said to drop. I called this "not a rotation problem — a shape mismatch", because my coarse search's best and runner-up tied at 0.552 and refinement stalled at 0.692. That was wrong. The pose is prerot_x −90°, pitch 35°, my 24-cube search never reached it, and with the correct rotation not one pixel of the mesh falls outside the video object.

teapot_ceramic_crack

Guan 2.18% uncovered · IoU 0.6819   mine 8.41% · IoU 0.6767

Rescued by the coverage gate, not by a better pose. Read the two numbers against each other: IoU is a dismal 0.682, yet only 2.18% of the mesh sits outside the video. Both are true. The video has a heavy cast shadow that inflates its mask, which craters symmetric IoU while leaving coverage untouched — a shadow can only ever ADD to the video side. My search chased that shadow and ended at 8.41% uncovered, worse than where it started.

teapot_porcelain

Guan 2.23% uncovered · IoU 0.8980   mine 3.19% · IoU 0.9069

Both correct, his slightly tighter. Same mesh and same rotation as ceramic_crack, on a clean white background. His pose leaves 2.23% uncovered against my 3.19%.

penguin_circuits

Guan 1.51% uncovered · IoU 0.8661   mine 2.01% · IoU 0.8689

Effectively tied. His 1.51% against my 2.01%. Both are the same pose to within a degree of refinement.

horse_metal

Guan 5.12% uncovered · IoU 0.8416   mine 3.56% · IoU 0.8708

Mine is slightly tighter here. My solve leaves 3.56% uncovered against his 5.12%. Not a contradiction — his rotation is the true pose from a fov-30 / dist-2.6 camera, and ours is fov-40 / dist-2. The pose is right; the framing differs, which is exactly why he recommends seeding the refine rather than using the raw matrix.

whale_spots

Guan 2.00% uncovered · IoU 0.8038   mine 1.34% · IoU 0.8202

Mine slightly tighter, both pass. 1.34% against 2.00%. Same story as the horse — a camera-framing difference, not a pose error.

Every frame: ground truth, the 2D copy, and backprojection

All six rebuilt on Guan's rotation, then played end to end. Three panels: ground truth (the raw video frame) · 2D copy (option B, screen space — what the loss is actually scored against) · backprojection (option C, colour pushed out to the mesh's vertices and re-rendered).

What to watch for

The video frames are untouched — what the rotation changes is which video pixels fall inside our silhouette, and so what the loss ever sees. Two things are visible only in motion: the rim fill growing as the video model reshapes the object over the clip, and cast shadows sitting in the left panel while never entering the target.

pumpkin_rot

219,379 px · 121 frames · 100.0–100.0% straight from video · 0 white px

The object I had written off as unfixable. 100.0% of every target is a direct copy — not one pixel of rim fill on any frame.

Two new objects, generated for the lava set

Both shot against the same fixed camera and rebuilt on Guan's rotations. Two panels here, not three: ground truth (raw video frame) · 2D copy (what the loss is scored against). These exist to give the multi-shape training more than two lava shapes — previously only spot and teapot had the effect.

Why the prompt had to change twice

The first pumpkin clip asked for "embers drifting up from the hottest seams" and "heat shimmer above the cracks". Both are off-surface effects by definition, and adding "must not cross the mesh boundary" does not undo them — video models follow the positive nouns and largely ignore negations. The fix was to delete those clauses rather than negate them, leaving only magma creeping inside the fissures and cracks brightening and cooling.

One clause still costs us: "brightening to white-hot". White-hot reads as background under the near-white threshold, which is where pumpkin's worst frame loses 11,400 px of coverage. Next clip should say vivid orange.

horse_lava

132,651 px · 150 frames · 95.5–100.0% straight from video · 0 white px

The cleaner of the two. 99.3% of target pixels come straight from the video, rim fill never exceeds 5,970 px, and IoU never drops below 0.919 — the effect stayed on the body.

pumpkin_lava

219,379 px · 150 frames · 94.4–100.0% straight from video · 0 white px

Generated from the corrected prompt, then measured. Its video silhouette grows 70.6% across the clip — glow spilling past the rind into the background. That never reaches the target: the copy is stencilled by the mesh, so the spill is discarded. It is why the rim fill peaks at 12,331 px and why IoU falls to 0.534 while coverage stays 100%.

Coverage, not IoU — again

pumpkin_lava is the second case on this page where the two metrics disagree sharply and coverage is the one that is right. Its IoU bottoms out at 0.534, which reads like a registration failure. It is not: the video's glow simply extends past the rind, and every one of those pixels is outside our silhouette and therefore never scored. Coverage stays at 100% for all 150 frames. Judging this clip on IoU would have thrown away a usable object.

Net effect

My search: 4 of 6 usable. With Guan's rotations and the coverage gate: 6 of 6. He also supplies rotations for five objects whose videos do not exist yet — hammer, armadillo, batman, hat, cow — and has wired the export into his renderer, so no future object needs a search.

On the three where my search is marginally tighter (horse 3.56% vs 5.12%, whale 1.34% vs 2.00%, penguin 2.01% vs 1.51%), the cause is camera framing, not pose: his Kling renders are fov 30 at distance 2.6, ours is fov 40 at distance 2. His recommendation stands — seed the refine with his rotation and drop the 24-cube coarse search.
